text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

R. v. Newman,

2013 BCSC 592

Date: 20130220

Docket:
25031

Registry: Vancouver

Regina

v.

Michael Bruce Newman

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice Ehrcke

Oral Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Crown:

G.C.
Proulx

E. Leno

Counsel for the Accused:

J.M.
Peters

M. Vis-Dunbar

Place and Date of Trial:

Vancouver,
B.C.

October 15-19,22-26,29-31, 2012

November 5-9,13,19-23,26-30, 2012

December 3-7,10-12, 2012

January 14-18,21-25,28-31, 2013

February 1 and 4, 2013

Place and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver,
B.C.

February 20, 2013

Introduction

[
1
]

THE COURT:
Sometime
around noon on Tuesday, January 6, 2004, Marc Rozen was killed in his apartment
on Haro Street in Vancouver, British Columbia. For more than three years
thereafter, no one was charged with the killing.

[
2
]

On March 29, 2007, Michael Newman was arrested
in Vaughan, Ontario, on drug charges. The following day there was an apparent
break-in at Mr. Newman's residence in Ontario. The investigation of those
matters led the Ontario police to exchange certain information with the
Vancouver police, which eventually led to Mr. Newman being charged with
the first degree murder of Marc Rozen.

[
3
]

The Indictment reads as follows:

Michael Bruce NEWMAN stands charged that

Count 1

Michael Bruce
NEWMAN, on or about the 6th day of January, 2004 at or near Vancouver, in the
Province of British Columbia, did commit the first degree murder of Marc Rozen,
contrary to
Section 235(1)
of the
Criminal Code of Canada
.

[
4
]

Mr. Newman elected to be tried by Supreme
Court Judge alone. At the beginning of this trial, it appeared that the live
issues would include whether the evidence established beyond a reasonable doubt
that Mr. Newman was present in Marc Rozen's apartment at the time of his death.
The Crown led a great deal of evidence to establish that fact. During the
defence case, Mr. Newman took the witness stand and admitted that he was
at Mr. Rozen's apartment, but said he took no part in his killing. Consequently,
the major issue now before me is what role, if any, Mr. Newman played in
causing Marc Rozen's death, and whether the Crown has proven his culpability
for first degree murder beyond a reasonable doubt.

[
5
]

It is useful to state at the outset that the
accused is presumed to be innocent unless and until the Crown proves his guilt
beyond a reasonable doubt. That onus remains on the Crown throughout and never
shifts. The accused has no onus of proving anything.

[
6
]

As the Supreme Court of Canada explained in
R.
v.

W.(D.)
,
1991 CanLII 93 (SCC)
, [1991] 1 S.C.R. 742, if I, as the trier of fact, believe Mr. Newman's
testimony that he did not commit the offence charged, I must find him not
guilty. Second, even if I do not believe his testimony, I must find him not
guilty if his testimony leaves me with a reasonable doubt about his guilt. Finally,
even if Mr. Newman's evidence does not raise a reasonable doubt about his
guilt, I must go on to ask myself whether, on the basis of all the evidence, I
am satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt of Mr. Newman's guilt. I am required
to find Mr. Newman not guilty if, after considering all the evidence, I am
not convinced that the Crown has satisfied its onus of proving his guilt beyond
a reasonable doubt.

[
7
]

I shall not in these reasons recite all the
testimony of every witness or describe every exhibit, although I have carefully
considered them all in reaching my verdict. Over 65 witnesses were called by
the Crown at trial. The defence called several witnesses, including Mr. Newman.
More than 280 exhibits were filed. What follows is a summary of some of the
more important aspects of the evidence led at trial, but I repeat that my
verdict is based on a consideration of the whole of the evidence and not merely
on this summary.

Background Events Prior to Marc Rozen's Death

[
8
]

Marc Rozen was a strong, healthy young man at
the time of his death in January 2004. He was about six feet tall and weighed
about 235 pounds. The autopsy report listed his age as 38 years.

[
9
]

In July 2002, Mr. Rozen became engaged to
Paige Kerr, and he gave her a platinum engagement ring with a single solitaire
diamond, as shown in the photographs of Exhibit 27. An invoice has been marked
as Exhibit 263 showing that Mr. Rozen bought the .91 carat diamond ring in
the State of Washington for $2,800 on July 17, 2002.

[
10
]

In October 2002, Ms. Kerr and Marc Rozen
began travelling together, including a trip to Israel. They returned to Canada
in May 2003 and then moved to California where she had obtained employment. Shortly
thereafter, in July 2003, their engagement ended. She returned the ring, and he
brought it back with him to Canada.

[
11
]

Ms. Kerr described Marc Rozen as a strong
young man, who exercised regularly. She said he had a silver mezuzah or pendant
on a chain around his neck with a Hebrew prayer inside of it, which he always
wore, even when sleeping or showering. He dressed casually, often wearing dark
tear-away track pants with white stripes on the leg. He usually wore slippers
indoors. She did not know him to have a gold watch. She said he was always
friendly and open with new people. He liked the process of bargaining or
negotiating, and when doing so, he was authoritative without being aggressive,
and he was never violent.

[
12
]

She spoke to him a few times on the telephone in
the fall of 2003. The last phone call was in December 2003, at which time he
seemed happy and settled in his life.

[
13
]

Marc Rozen signed a rental agreement for Suite
1106, 1816 Haro Street, Vancouver, British Columbia, on August 27, 2003, and he
moved in on September 1, 2003. The rental agent, Chris Sherry, described him as
a courteous, polite, and intelligent young man. She gave him two sets of keys. During
the time he lived there, she said she received one noise complaint from a
neighbour, but she said that was not unusual.

[
14
]

Mr. Rozen went out with a number of young
women in the summer and fall of 2003.

[
15
]

Rochel Tucker dated Marc Rozen from the end of
August until the beginning of October 2003, when she went to India. She helped
him move into his apartment, and she lived there with him for a period of time.
He gave her a set of keys, which she returned to him when she left. She helped
him paint the apartment. They painted the spare bedroom purple, and throughout
these reasons, I shall refer to that as the purple room. The purple room
contained a futon bed, a tall floor lamp, and a table or desk for the computer
and cordless phone.

[
16
]

Ms. Tucker had seen the engagement ring,
which Mr. Rozen kept in a jumble drawer in the kitchen, across from the
sink. At that time, Mr. Rozen did not have regular employment. She
described the clothing he typically wore, including a dark navy knee-length
coat and snap-open pants with a stripe along the leg.

[
17
]

Ms. Tucker described Marc Rozen as being
passionate about social change and interested in troubled youth. She said he
was friendly to everyone and gave food to street people. She never saw him
violent with anyone, although he was big and strong.

[
18
]

Her last contact with him was a long phone call
just before New Year's, at which time he seemed happy. He did not express any
concerns about enemies, nor did he say that he was fearful of anyone.

[
19
]

Wayne Bishop is a gemologist for John Bishop
Jewellers Ltd. who prepared an appraisal of the diamond engagement ring for
Marc Rozen at the end of November 2003. The appraisal, in the amount of
$18,000, is marked as Exhibit 21, and the ring is shown in the photographs in
Exhibit 27. Mr. Bishop polished the ring, and Mr. Rozen picked it up
on November 27, 2003. Mr. Rozen told Mr. Bishop that he intended to
sell the ring, and he was trying to get as much for it as he could. Mr. Bishop
said that on a private sale the price might be only about half of the appraised
value.

[
20
]

Keonna Brisdon dated Marc Rozen from the end of
October until Christmas, 2003. He never gave her a set of keys. He carried his
keys on a lanyard around his neck. She described the dark-coloured winter coat
that he wore, and she said he kept it in the closet in the purple spare
bedroom.

[
21
]

He showed her the engagement ring, but she did
not know where he kept it. She helped him write an ad for it which they called
in to a newspaper before Christmas. She identified Exhibit 30 as a
Vancouver
Sun
classified ad for the ring that ran on January 3, 2004. There were also
ads in the
Georgia Straight
and the
Buy and Sell
, marked as
Exhibits 229 and 230, which mentioned the $18,000 appraisal, but offered the
ring at a price of $8,900. On Christmas Day they had an argument and split up. Although
there were raised voices, Mr. Rozen never struck her or used physical
violence.

[
22
]

Ann Marie Kraft knew Marc Rozen since the 1990s,
and they had friends in common. In 1999, they both worked for Katimavik, a
Canadian youth volunteer program, but then she moved away. She ran into him
again in the fall of 2003, and she saw him at a Christmas party in December. From
then until the New Year they spent a lot of time together, but on January 1,
2004, they had a discussion that went “sideways”, and she walked out. She said
he was never physically violent with her, although he had a temper and
sometimes got upset when he thought people were making fun of him. She
described an incident when some old acquaintances made fun of him for being
Jewish. She was not aware of his ever receiving any threats.

[
23
]

She said that Marc Rozen used to wear a dark
navy thigh-length wool coat, which she believes he kept in the closet in the
purple room. He did not wear shoes in his apartment.

[
24
]

Andrew Strang is a friend who had known Marc
Rozen since grade school. They played sports together, but drifted apart when
they both went to law school. They reconnected at a friend's marriage and a
reunion in 2003. He described Marc Rozen as happy-go-lucky. However, in
mid-December 2003, they both attended a funeral, and Marc Rozen was very
emotional.

[
25
]

Mr. Strang said Marc Rozen was as strong as
an ox, but he did not show it. He never saw Marc Rozen fight, but he was
confident when playing sports and would stand up for himself.

[
26
]

After Marc Rozen's death, the police allowed Mr. Strang
to enter his apartment, Number 1106. Neither the engagement ring, nor the dark
winter coat that Mr. Rozen used to wear were ever found.

[
27
]

David Levinson knew Marc Rozen since the 1980s,
and they reconnected in the fall of 2003. Marc Rozen was a Canucks fan and went
to a game with Mr. Levinson on January 5, 2004, using a special media
pass, as depicted in Exhibit 31, which shows the pass on a lanyard with keys.
Mr. Levinson drove him home after the game. Mr. Rozen was in good
spirits and said, "I'll see you tomorrow." He did not express any
fears. Mr. Levinson asked him if he could stay because he needed some help
the next morning, but Mr. Rozen said he could not because he had a meeting
set up then to sell his engagement ring, and he could not cancel the meeting. He
did not give Mr. Levinson any information about who he was expecting to
meet, whether it was a man or a woman, the number of people, the time, or how
the meeting was arranged, but he did not seem fearful.

Events on January 6, 2004

[
28
]

The first person to call the police about
suspicious activities on the eleventh floor of the apartment at 1816 Haro
Street was Rick Prodanuk, who lived in Suite 1102. He testified that he was
watching a DVD in his living room when he heard a couple of male voices that he
thought were coming from Suite 1103 next door. It sounded to him like someone
trying to get in -- commotion at the door. He heard two to three minutes of
thumping, and the voices got louder. It sounded like the door flew open and hit
the door stop. The door closed and the voices were muffled. There was more loud
arguing, but he could not hear the words. It sounded like a wrestling match,
with furniture being thrown around for two or three minutes, and then it was
quiet for a few minutes, after which the sounds resumed again. This happened
two or three times over a 10 to 15-minute period. About 8 to 10 minutes in, he
heard a loud and frantic voice, which he recognized as the voice of Marc Rozen,
saying, "Why are you doing this to me?" Then he heard a loud shriek,
like a high-pitched woman's voice. There was more thumping, and then another
shriek.

[
29
]

After the second shriek, he called 9-1-1. He
thought his call was around noon, but police logs introduced through the EComm
voice records co-ordinator, Sandi Greenfield, show the actual time of the call
was 12:57 p.m. Mr. Prodanuk told the 9‑1‑1 operator that it
sounded like a break-in, with banging and crashing and a woman yelling a bit,
and that he thought it was next door at Suite 1103, where a Chinese couple
lived. The operator asked if it was a break-in or a domestic dispute, and he
said he did not know.

[
30
]

When the police eventually arrived, he directed
them to Suite 1103, but after they spoke to the Chinese residents and
determined there was no problem there, they went to Suite 1106 and saw blood on
carpet. Mr. Prodanuk thought the door to 1106 was not locked when the
police tried to enter, but I find as a fact that he is mistaken in that regard,
as it contradicts other reliable evidence.

[
31
]

Mr. Prodanuk recalled an earlier occasion
when he overheard Mr. Rozen arguing with Barbara Darovski in Suite 1105. At
that time, he heard Mr. Rozen say, "Barb, you've been riding me since
I moved in here; now you're complaining about my cupboards slamming too
loud."

[
32
]

The second person to call the police was the
building's caretaker, Srdjan Cosovic, who lived on the ground floor in Suite
101 with his wife and child. He was shovelling snow on January 6, 2004, when
his wife told him that Barbara Darovski in Suite 1105 had called and left a
message. He listened to the message, which reported that someone was fighting
in Suite 1106. He called 9‑1‑1 at 12:59 p.m. and told the operator
he was the building manager and that a tenant from the eleventh floor had
reported fighting and someone screaming for help in Suite 1106. When the
operator asked how the police would get in the building, he said he would wait
for them at the front door.

[
33
]

Mr. Cosovic went to the lobby, and while
he waited for the police, the mailman came. About 15 to 25 minutes after his 9‑1‑1
call, he saw a white male step out of the west elevator. There were also two
older ladies who remained in the elevator, 70-year-old Flora McDonald and
another older woman. The man walked to the exit door toward Haro Street and
turned right toward Denman. The man was holding a white towel around his neck
like a scarf and leaned to the right and touched his head, as if he were
injured. His face was shiny, as if he had cream on his face. Mr. Cosovic
described him as a white male, 28 to 34 years of age, slim build, high cheek
bones, sharp chin, wearing brown shoes, blue pants, a black winter thigh-length
coat, and a black toque, similar to the coat and toque he had seen Marc Rozen
wear on previous occasions. The man was not a tenant, and Mr. Cosovic had
never seen him before. According to Mr. Cosovic, the man was carrying a
white plastic bag with green markings in his left hand. He said it was not a
gym bag. It was either empty or had something light in it. There were no stains
on the man's body or clothing, but there was blood in front of and in the
elevator. There was also blood on the carpet in front of the door to 1106, so Mr. Cosovic
called 9‑1‑1 again at 1:39 p.m.

[
34
]

About five minutes after the second 9‑1‑1
call, he started shovelling snow again. The police came and he showed them the
blood. The police said they were there to investigate Suite 1103, but he told
them it was 1106. They knocked on 1106, but there was no answer. The door was
locked with a deadbolt. Mr. Cosovic looked for the key, but it was his
wife who eventually found it. He used the key to unlock and open the door of 1106,
but he did not go in. He could see blood everywhere and drywall damaged. The
police radioed for more help. He locked the elevator that had the blood in it. He
gave the police his description of the man he had seen leaving the building.

[
35
]

A few days later, Mr. Cosovic met with a
police sketch artist, Sergeant Flewelling, who produced a sketch that he
forwarded to the investigators. That sketch has been marked as Exhibit 8.
Mr. Cosovic said it is a good rendering of the image in his mind of the
man he saw leaving the building. At various times the police showed him photo
lineups, but he never selected anyone. Interestingly, a photograph of Mr. Newman
was included in the photo-pack lineup shown to Mr. Cosovic on July 25,
2006, but he did not select Mr. Newman. He testified that the accused in
court looks like the man he saw, but he could not be 100% sure.

[
36
]

Nevertheless, there can now be no doubt that the
man seen by Mr. Cosovic was in fact Mr. Newman, because Mr. Newman
has testified that he saw Mr. Cosovic and the postman in the lobby when he
left the elevator and walked out the front door of the building on January 6,
2004.

[
37
]

Initially, many of the police officers who
viewed the scene, including Constable Deighton and Detective Phillips, were
under the impression that there may have been four types of footprints in the
apartment, and that therefore there may have been three people present in
addition to Mark Rozen.

[
38
]

On January 23, 2004, Detective Phillips put up
an Information Wanted poster in the lobby of 1816 Haro Street, which said that
police believed two males and one female were involved in the murder. When Mr. Cosovic
saw this, he told Detective Phillips very forcefully, "No, there was only
one involved in the murder." He said he only saw one person who did not
belong in the building.

[
39
]

However, Mr. Cosovic testified that some
time later, it “came into his head” that he had seen a couple leave the
building. He did not pay much attention to them. They were not tenants, and he
was not sure if they were visiting someone or related. He thought the man was
about six feet tall and in his mid-thirties and the woman was around five feet
tall with curly hair that was not blond. He thought she was wearing a dark red
coat with black spots on it. He testified that he saw no blood or injuries on
them and they walked quickly with no indication of any injury. He is unsure of
the time in relation to his 9‑1‑1 calls, but he thought it could
have been 30 to 45 minutes before he saw the injured man leave. He gave this
information to Detective Nixon on July 17, 2006. Earlier, on February 20, 2004,
Mr. Cosovic mentioned to Detective Phillips that he had seen a couple
leaving the building before he phoned 9‑1‑1, but Detective Phillips
did not obtain a description from him.

[
40
]

Barbara Darovski is the tenant who lived in
Suite 1105, adjacent to Mr. Rozen's apartment, 1106. She had had arguments
with Mr. Rozen in the past when she complained about noise from his
apartment.

[
41
]

Ms. Darovski testified that as she was
making lunch on January 6, 2004, around 12:40 p.m., she heard loud bangs on her
dining room wall, which is adjacent to the front door of Suite 1106. The mirror
on her wall was shaking. She heard no voices prior to this. The banging lasted
five minutes, then stopped and started again a few minutes later for five
minutes. The sounds then moved to the wall of her living room, which is
adjacent to the dining room of Mr. Rozen's apartment. It sounded like
furniture moving. She heard voices that sounded like a woman scared of a mouse.
Then she heard the word "Help", and it sounded like Marc Rozen's
voice. She was very afraid and called Mr. Cosovic to ask him to call the
police.

[
42
]

She looked through the peephole in her front
door and saw no one. Then, around 1:15 to 1:20 p.m., she looked again when she
heard the click of the lock on the door of Suite 1106. She saw a person who she
thought looked smaller than herself, with a slight build, wearing a dark toque,
dark clothing and trousers with a stripe on the pant leg. She could not see the
face or hair of the person. She was unsure if it was a man or a woman, but she
had the impression it was a woman. About 10 to 15 minutes later, Dick Snater
left his apartment, 1104, and went down the stairs.

[
43
]

Although Ms. Darovski had the impression
that the person she saw through her peephole was a woman, I find as a fact it
was Mr. Newman. Mr. Cosovic saw Mr. Newman come out of the
elevator 15 to 25 minutes after his first 9‑1‑1 call, which was at
12:59 p.m. That puts Mr. Newman in the lobby at around 1:14 to 1:24 p.m.,
which corresponds with Ms. Darovski's observation of the person locking
the door of Suite 1106 at 1:15 to 1:20 p.m. As well, the person she saw was
wearing dark clothing and a dark toque, which matches Mr. Cosovic's
description of Mr. Newman when he came out of the elevator, except for the
fact that Mr. Cosovic thought he was wearing blue pants. I find this
discrepancy to be insignificant, given that Mr. Cosovic was mistaken in
another detail, namely his impression that the injured person had cream on his
face, which we know from Mr. Newman's testimony to be incorrect. Although Ms. Darovski
thought the person locking the door was shorter than herself, this may be
explained by the distorting effect of the lens in the peephole, as observed by
Constable Rogers, who looked through the peephole when she took a statement
from Ms. Darovski. Constable Rogers said the peephole had a fisheye lens
that made things appear smaller than they really are.

[
44
]

Constable Rogers also took a tape-recorded
statement from Dick Snater in his apartment, 1104, on January 6, 2004 at 6:00
p.m. Unfortunately, Mr. Snater died prior to the trial. I admitted his
statement in evidence as an exception to the rule against hearsay, as defence
counsel agreed that the requirement of necessity was met and he did not contest
the statement's reliability. In considering the weight to attach to his
statement, I take into account the fact that it was not under oath and there
was no opportunity to cross-examine Mr. Snater. In the statement, a
transcript of which was marked Exhibit 227, Mr. Snater said:

. . .
I heard a fight in terms of people being banged against walls. Uh, uh and
there, there was a female voice, a young female voice at one point but I cannot
tell you at what point. But there was a female voice who was likely a younger
person. And um I heard I may have heard male voices that I cannot remember and
um what I heard were 2 or 3 different incidents of a physical fight of people
being smacked against a wall type of thing . . . And each time I
check the peep hole there was no sound and the door is closed. Then a few
minutes later there is another uproar with the same sounds of people being
smacked to the door or to the wall or, or door as far as that goes.

[
45
]

Mr. Snater explained that he did not want
to get involved. He then went on to say:

And I feel like
a heel but I just turned off the television and I just pretended I wasn't home
but I did hear again another incident of, of the banging against like the
slamming of a body against a wall is what it sounded like. And I think that's
either that's when I heard the female voice or the last 2 of the 3 incidents I
heard the female voice. I think I heard her twice on 2 different occasions but
only briefly. And honestly I think that's and then I had an appointment at, at
to meet people so I, I heard nothing else and when I left, I came out my front
door and I didn't want to be, I didn't want to see any damage done it sounded
like something might have happened out front so I went down or uh up the stairs . . .

[
46
]

Mr. Snater said he noticed a couple of
orange stains in front of 1106, and he knew the sounds had been coming from
1106. He said the incidents were on and off, less than a minute each, over a
period of 10 to 15 minutes in total. He described the female voice in this way:

. . .
it wasn't hysterical it was like an, an urging like okay enough or something
like that. But, but that those weren't necessarily the words but it wasn't an,
an hysterical screaming it was like, like a, a managed voice.

[
47
]

Mr. Snater said he could not remember if he
heard a male voice at all. As to the words spoken by the female, he said:

It was like um
like, like 10 words you know like okay, okay that's enough already or something
like that and I'm just using an example. Um, um that wasn't at all it but uh
but um, um as an example you know just that kind of vocabulary.

[
48
]

Constables Foster and McMillan of the Vancouver
Police Department arrived at 1816 Haro Street at 2:15 p.m. They were the first
officers on the scene. They spoke to Mr. Prodanuk, then checked Suite 1103
and confirmed there was no problem there. They spoke to Mr. Cosovic in the
lobby and then went to the door of 1106. There was a red smudge on the carpet. They
knocked, but there was no response. Mr. Cosovic's keys did not work, but
then his wife found keys to unlock the deadbolt. When they entered the suite at
2:43 p.m., they saw large amounts of blood on the walls and floor. As they
entered, they tried to avoid stepping in the blood, and when they left, they tried
to retrace their steps.

[
49
]

Constable Foster went no further than the
kitchen, which is just off the entrance hallway to the left. There is a closet
with no door just to the right of the entrance hallway, and just beyond that on
the right side of the hallway is the bathroom. Further down the entrance
hallway on the right is the purple room. The entrance hallway runs north-south,
with the front door of the suite at the south end. At the north end of the
entrance hallway is the master bedroom. An east-west hallway connects with the
entrance hallway at this point. It leads to a large room, the north end of
which was used as the living room, and the south end of which was the dining
room, with a sliding glass door leading to a small balcony or patio. The narrow
kitchen connects with the dining room at the west end, and with the entrance
hall at the east end. In effect, the kitchen could be considered a type of
hallway, parallel to the east-west hallway, connecting the entrance area near
the front door with the dining room.

[
50
]

Constable McMillan walked up the left side of
the entrance hallway, checking to ensure that no one else was in the apartment.
In the living room, he found Marc Rozen lying on his back, arms outstretched to
the sides, with no pulse. Constable McMillan observed that he had a large gash
to the right side of his neck and a cut to his left calf. There was a four-inch
paring knife with a black handle lying on his upper chest. He was barefoot.

[
51
]

One set of keys to the apartment was found by
the front door. No other keys were ever found.

[
52
]

Dean Simmens, an Emergency Health Services
attendant, entered the suite at 2:48 p.m. and confirmed that Marc Rozen was
dead.

[
53
]

Sergeant Kodak arrived at 2:50 p.m., took
control of the crime scene, and the investigation began. A description of the
injured suspect, as observed by Mr. Cosovic, was broadcast. Officers
checked the parkade and the area outside the building for evidence. They
checked for video surveillance evidence, but nothing useful was obtained. Area
hospitals and medical clinics were alerted to be on the lookout for the injured
suspect who may be seeking treatment for a knife wound, but without results.

[
54
]

Over the course of the following week, the
Vancouver Police conducted a thorough examination of the crime scene pursuant
to a warrant.

The Autopsy

[
55
]

The coroner, Steven Fonseca, attended 1816 Haro
Street at 10:13 p.m. on January 6, 2004, to remove Marc Rozen's body from Suite
1106. His usual practice would have been to don a protective suit and
protective booties so as not to contaminate the scene, but in this case he has
no precise recollection of whether he did so. Comparing the soles of the shoes
he was wearing that day, it now appears that he may be responsible for at least
one of the shoe impressions that the police later found at the scene; namely, a
shoe print on the carpet in the living room where he would have been standing
when removing the body. During his testimony, Mr. Fonseca drew a circle
around that area of the carpet on Photograph KK-05 of Exhibit 78.

[
56
]

Both Sergeant Hamilton and Constable Deighton
were present when the coroner removed the body on January 6, 2004. While

Analysis of the Evidence in Accordance with
R. v.
W.(D.)

[
267
]

I have considered carefully the testimony of Mr. Newman and the
other defence witnesses in the context of the whole of the evidence. I can say
without hesitation that I do not accept the exculpatory parts of Mr. Newman's
evidence as true, nor do they raise any reasonable doubt in my mind as to his
guilt. On the contrary, I am convinced beyond a reasonable doubt that the
exculpatory parts of Mr. Newman's testimony are false and were
deliberately fabricated by him to mislead the Court as to his responsibility
for this crime.

[
268
]

That does not mean that I reject every statement made by Mr. Newman
in his testimony. As with the testimony of any witness, the trier of fact may
accept all, part, or none of the accused’s evidence. While I reject Mr. Newman's
claim that he never assaulted Mr. Rozen, and while I reject generally his
account about the participation of the unknown male and unknown female, there
are a few aspects of his testimony that I accept as true. I accept as true his
admission that he was at Mr. Rozen's apartment at the time Mr. Rozen
was killed. I accept that he had made an appointment with Mr. Rozen to see
the ring. I accept his testimony that he was never unlawfully assaulted by Mr. Rozen.
I accept that he cleaned himself up and left his cream-coloured jacket in the
bathroom. I accept that he wore Mr. Rozen's dark coat and toque when he
left the apartment. I accept that he took the two guns and the silencer with
him. I accept that he was the last person to leave the apartment.

[
269
]

I reject as false and as a deliberate fabrication by Mr. Newman
his claim that there was a man and a woman in the apartment who were unknown to
him and who assaulted both him and Mr. Rozen. I reject his claim that they
were the ones who introduced the firearms and silencer into the apartment
without his participation. I find that if there was a man and a woman in the
apartment, they were associates of Mr. Newman and came to the apartment
with him, and that Mr. Newman was the person who supplied the guns and the
silencer that were used in the assault on Mr. Rozen.

[
270
]

There are numerous reasons why I reject as false and as fabricated
the exculpatory aspects of Mr. Newman's testimony. I cannot list every one
of those reasons here. I shall highlight some of the important factors that
lead me to this conclusion, but this list should not be considered exhaustive.

[
271
]

First, if Mr. Newman had been assaulted as he testified, he
would have taken advantage of the multiple opportunities he had to flee the
apartment, as this would have brought the assault against him to an end.
Mr. Newman agreed in his testimony that he passed up more than one
opportunity to flee. Instead of fleeing when he had the chance, he testified
that he went after the male attacker. This simply makes no sense. Mr. Newman
said that he and Mr. Rozen were perfect strangers, so why would he stay to
engage in this fight with an unknown man who was apparently stronger than he
was? Even if he was motivated to help Mr. Rozen from the attack by the
unknown man, Mr. Newman could have helped far more effectively by fleeing
the apartment and summoning the assistance of others. After all, Mr. Newman
knew that one of the assailants had a gun, and if Mr. Newman was unarmed,
he was no match for that.

[
272
]

Second, I find that if the unknown man and woman had supplied the
firearms and had used them to kill Mr. Rozen and shoot Mr. Newman,
then they would not have left the weapons in the apartment when they left. As Mr. Newman
himself testified, those guns were a "calling card" for the assailants,
from which they might be traced, either by forensic toolmark testing of the
guns, or by fingerprints, or by DNA, or by tracing the origin of the guns by
their serial numbers. It is completely unbelievable that they would have
deliberately left the guns behind if they had been the assailants, as Mr. Newman
testified.

[
273
]

Third, if the man and the woman had killed Mr. Rozen without
the participation of Mr. Newman, they would not have left the apartment
without first being sure that Mr. Newman would not be able to testify
against them if they were caught. On Mr. Newman's account, the man and
woman would have known that he was an eyewitness to their crimes. If they were
prepared to kill Mr. Rozen, they would not have left Mr. Newman alive
in the apartment to implicate them.

[
274
]

Fourth, I consider Mr. Newman's own conduct immediately after Mr. Rozen
was killed. This may fall into the category of so-called
"after-the-fact" evidence, or "post-offence conduct". Such
evidence must be approached with caution, because often there may be an
explanation for the conduct other than consciousness of guilt. People often do
things out of fear or panic, even though they may be innocent. For example,
they may fear that no one would believe their innocent explanation, even though
it may be true.

[
275
]

With that in mind, I place little significance on the evidence of Mr. Newman's
conduct in the months and years after the killing. This includes evidence of
his moving to Ontario and his using a name other than his true name. There
could be many reasons for this that are unrelated to this killing.

[
276
]

However, I find the events that took place in the minutes and hours
immediately following the killing are very significant, because I find that
they are completely inconsistent with Mr. Newman's testimony that he was
himself the victim of an assault in Mr. Rozen's apartment.

[
277
]

According to Mr. Newman's testimony, he was shot by the woman
and stabbed by the unknown man in the apartment, and his injuries were so
serious that he thought he was going to die. Yet when he discovered that the
assailants were gone, he did not seek medical help, either for himself or for Mr. Rozen.

[
278
]

There were two women in the elevator Mr. Newman took to the
lobby. Why did he not tell them what had happened and ask them to call an ambulance?

[
279
]

Then, when he arrived at the lobby and exited the elevator, Mr. Newman
saw both the postman and Mr. Cosovic. Why did he not ask them to get
medical help for himself and Mr. Rozen?

[
280
]

Not only did he refrain from asking these people for help, but he
also did everything in his power to hide from them the fact that he was injured.
That is why he cleaned himself up in Mr. Rozen's bathroom, and why he
wrapped a towel around his neck, and why he discarded his bloody jacket in
preference for Mr. Rozen's coat when he left the building.

[
281
]

I find that this conduct is completely inconsistent with Mr. Newman's
testimony that he had been the victim of an unlawful assault in the apartment. On
the contrary, it is consistent with Mr. Newman's awareness that he had himself
committed a terrible, violent crime in the apartment for which he wanted to
avoid detection.

[
282
]

The same may be said of the treatment of his wounds in the office of
Dr. Gentis instead of seeking treatment in hospital. On Mr. Newman's
testimony, he had been the innocent victim of a gunshot wound at the hands of a
dangerous assailant. On his account, he was innocent of any wrongdoing. Why
then would he not go to hospital to receive treatment for this and other
wounds? Why would he leave it to a friend to remove the bullet in his
apartment? Why would Dr. Gentis be paid in cash? There is evidence in this
trial that Mr. Newman had MSP coverage at the time, so he could have had
treatment by skilled physicians in hospital at no cost. Why would he trust a
friend to remove the bullet? Why would he take a chance on treatment in a
doctor's office instead of hospital for the wounds he believed to be so serious
that he thought he was going to die? We know that he did not have a general
aversion to hospitals, because there is evidence that he was treated for a hand
wound in St. Paul's Hospital one year later, in 2005.

[
283
]

I find this conduct to be completely inconsistent with Mr. Newman's
testimony that he was the innocent victim of an assault. On the contrary, it is
consistent with his consciousness that he had himself committed a terrible
crime, and he did not want his injuries to become known, for fear that this
would create a trail of evidence leading back to his involvement in the killing
at Mr. Rozen's apartment.

[
284
]

Finally, I find it incredible that if Mr. Newman had been the
innocent victim of an assault and shooting in the apartment, he would then
remove the weapons from the apartment and take steps to ensure that their
whereabouts remained hidden. By doing so, he deprived the authorities of an
important piece of evidence. That is not the conduct of an innocent victim of
violent crime. It is more consistent with the conduct of a perpetrator of such
crime.

[
285
]

For these and other reasons too plentiful to enumerate, I find that Mr. Newman's
testimony that he was an innocent victim of an assault in Mr. Rozen's
apartment at the hands of a man and a woman unknown to him, and that he himself
committed no assault on Mr. Rozen, is false, and does not raise a
reasonable doubt in my mind.

[
286
]

Having so concluded, I go on then to the third step discussed in
R.
v. W.(D.)
: Does the evidence considered as a whole prove Mr. Newman's
guilt beyond a reasonable doubt?

[
287
]

Upon a consideration of the evidence as a whole, I make the
following findings of fact.

[
288
]

Mr. Rozen was killed in his own apartment at 1106 - 1816 Haro
Street, Vancouver, British Columbia, sometime around noon on Tuesday, January
6, 2004.

[
289
]

The time and place of his death are not in dispute. There can be no
doubt that his death was caused by multiple gunshots and stab wounds. I accept
the finding in Dr. Lee's autopsy report that the principal cause of death
was gunshot and stab wounds of the head and neck.

[
290
]

The killing was accompanied by a theft of the diamond engagement
ring that Mr. Rozen had offered for sale in various newspapers. The
evidence of Mr. Levinson makes clear that the night before he died, Marc
Rozen was expecting to meet someone to sell the ring. After the killing, the
apartment was thoroughly searched, and neither the ring nor its documentation
could be found. I am satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that whoever killed
Marc Rozen also stole the ring.

[
291
]

Mr. Newman went to Marc Rozen's apartment shortly after noon on
January 6, 2004, to see the ring, having previously made an appointment with Mr. Rozen
to do so. This finding is consistent with what Mr. Newman admitted in his
testimony. Moreover, even apart from his testimony, there can be no doubt that
he was in Mr. Rozen's apartment that day. This conclusion is inescapable
from the fact that blood with Mr. Newman's DNA profile was found in
various places in the apartment. In addition, a piece of Mr. Newman's
flesh was found on the floor near the entrance to the purple room. The time
that Mr. Newman went there is established both by Mr. Newman's
testimony, and also by the evidence of the neighbours on the eleventh floor and
the time of the 9‑1‑1 calls.

[
292
]

In his trial testimony, Mr. Newman denied having a violent
confrontation with Mr. Rozen, but I have rejected that part of his
testimony as false and concocted. From the evidence I accept, I find beyond a
reasonable doubt that Mr. Newman did have a physical confrontation with Mr. Rozen
inside the apartment. This is the only reasonable inference to be drawn from
the following facts:  Mr. Newman's DNA was found in several locations on
the bloodstained shirt Mr. Rozen was wearing when police discovered his
dead body. In addition, a piece of chewing gum with Mr. Newman's DNA was
located on the sleeve of Mr. Rozen's shirt. As well, Mr. Rozen's DNA
was located in bloodstains on the left front pocket and rear collar of the
cream-coloured jacket that Mr. Newman had been wearing, and which he
discarded in the bathroom before leaving the apartment. A mixed profile DNA
from Mr. Rozen and Mr. Newman was found in a swab of blood from Mr. Rozen's
right hand and from nail clippings of his left hand as taken in the autopsy
(Exhibits 64 and 65). While any one of these circumstances individually
possibly might be explained away, when taken together I am satisfied they
establish beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Newman and Mr. Rozen
were in contact with each other and were struggling with each other. Moreover,
whoever else may have been in the apartment, Mr. Newman was the one most
thoroughly and actively engaged in the physical struggle with Mr. Rozen.

[
293
]

A woman was also present in the apartment during the confrontation. This
is established by the neighbours, all of whom heard a woman's voice. Mr. Prodanuk
said he heard a loud shriek, like a high-pitched woman's voice. Barbara
Darovski said she heard a voice like a woman scared of a mouse. Mr. Snater
said there was a young female voice on two occasions, saying something to the
effect of "that's enough already".

[
294
]

Whoever else was with Mr. Newman in Marc Rozen's apartment left
before Mr. Newman did. First, this is consistent with Mr. Newman's
admission during his testimony that he was the last person to leave the
apartment. Second, even apart from that, I have found as a fact that the person
Ms. Darovski saw locking the door of Suite 1106 at 1:15 to 1:20 p.m. was Mr. Newman.
No one else was with him at the time. To lock the door, he must have had one of
the two sets of keys, and he must have taken them with him. If anyone else had
still been inside the apartment after Mr. Newman left, they would have had
to unlock the door to get out. They then could not have re-locked the door,
because the only other set of keys was found by the police still inside the
apartment. Since the door to the apartment was locked when the police arrived,
it must have been locked by the last person who left, namely, Mr. Newman.

[
295
]

The woman in the apartment was not a friend of Marc Rozen. If she
had been, she would have sought help for him when she left the apartment prior
to Mr. Newman's leaving.

[
296
]

The only reasonable inference on all the evidence is that the woman
came to the apartment with Mr. Newman. The ring, after all, was a woman's
diamond ring. It would make sense for Mr. Newman to show up at Mr. Rozen's
apartment with a woman to look at the ring.

[
297
]

The more difficult question is whether there was another man
present, in addition to Mr. Rozen, Mr. Newman, and the unknown woman.
The footprint evidence as analyzed by Sergeant Hamilton suggests that in addition
to the barefoot impressions made by Mr. Rozen and the sockfoot impressions
made by Mr. Newman, there were also shoe impressions made by a man wearing
Hush Puppies. The existence of these different types of foot impressions led
the police investigators to develop the theory early on in the investigation
that there were three assailants, two men and one woman.

[
298
]

The theory of the Crown, however, is that the only male assailant
was Mr. Newman, and there was not another man present to attack Mr. Rozen.
The theory of the Crown is that after engaging in a bloody confrontation with Mr. Rozen,
and thereby making numerous bloody sockfoot impressions in the apartment, Mr. Newman
went to the bathroom to clean himself up, and he there put on the Hush Puppies
shoes before again walking around the apartment, perhaps to search for and
retrieve cartridge casings. In the Crown's theory, therefore, both the sockfoot
and the shoe impressions were created by Mr. Newman, and the woman did not
leave any bloody foot impressions because she left the suite before there was a
large accumulation of blood on the floor near the entrance door. In this way,
the Crown accounts for all the foot impressions, without the presence of an
unknown male assailant.

[
299
]

The theory of the Crown may well be correct. It is supported by the
fact that where there are both shoe and sock impressions at the same location,
the shoe impressions are on top of the sock impressions, consistent with the
Crown theory that Mr. Newman made the sock impressions first, and then
before leaving he put on the shoes and walked on top of some of his previous
sock impressions. The Crown theory is also supported by the fact that there
appear to be sockfoot impressions leading into the bathroom, but not leading
out. On the Crown's theory, this shows that Mr. Newman put his shoes on in
the bathroom.

[
300
]

As for the man and woman that Mr. Cosovic thinks he saw leaving
the building 30 to 45 minutes before the injured man, that is, Mr. Newman,
left the building, the Crown submits that this is a red herring. The Crown
submits that Mr. Cosovic was correct in his initial impression that these
people were either visiting or were relatives of another tenant, but in any
event, were not connected to the events in Suite 1106.

[
301
]

Were this a case to be decided on a balance of probabilities, I
would be inclined to accept the Crown's position that there was no other man
involved. However, as this is a criminal trial, the Crown bears the onus of
proving the accused's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. I find that I cannot
eliminate the possibility that there was another man present, even though I
find that possibility to be a remote one.

[
302
]

This leaves the question of who did what during the struggle in Marc
Rozen's apartment. Both the Crown and defence have put forward theories, and
both have tried to use the expert footprint evidence to support their scenario.
The defence theory is, of course, based on the testimony of Mr. Newman,
but defence counsel also tried to support that theory by submitting that it is
consistent with the footprint evidence and with the blood pattern evidence. Crown
counsel has put forward a different scenario of what happened and where, and
has submitted that its theory is supported by the footprint and blood pattern
evidence.

[
303
]

I find, however, that the expert footprint evidence is only a
limited tool in trying to understand what happened in that apartment. It leaves
many questions unanswered. One very noticeable problem is that the footprint
evidence clearly does not show everywhere that each of the participants walked
during the encounter. For one thing, persons who had not stepped in blood would
not have left prints. Second, a person may have been wearing footwear at one
time and not at another. For example, Marc Rozen may have been wearing flip
flops at one point, and at another point may have been barefoot. On the
footprint chart that was marked Exhibit 277, there are very few bloody barefoot
prints attributed to the deceased. There are a few of the deceased's barefoot
prints in the kitchen and one in the entrance to the master bedroom, which
leaves the question of how his body ended up in the living room. Another
problem is that there are either no, or very few, female footprints. Finally,
Exhibit 277 shows no prints near the overturned chair in the living room/dining
room, yet the bloodstains on that chair show that it was clearly a location
where Marc Rozen was being assaulted. So the footprint evidence only tells a
limited part of the story.

[
304
]

There are, however, some facts that are clearly established by the
DNA evidence and the blood pattern evidence. The first striking fact, which is
apparent from Exhibit 79, is that the blood and the DNA of both Marc Rozen and Mr. Newman
are found virtually throughout the apartment, with the exception of the master
bedroom. This demonstrates that those two men were involved in a struggle with
one other that moved from place to place in the apartment, in the purple room,
the entrance hallway particularly near the front door, through the kitchen, and
into both the dining room and the living room where the body of the deceased
was found.

[
305
]

Mr. Mellis said that in his opinion a person was sitting on the
dining room chair shown in Photograph KK-04 of Exhibit 78 before it was
overturned, and was bleeding into the cushion as he was sitting on it.

[
306
]

Second, according to Mr. Poon, the swab from the front edge of
the overturned chair in the living room tested positive for blood. The DNA was
a mixed profile, likely both male, from which Marc Rozen and Michael Newman
cannot be eliminated. The inclusion probability is one in 470,000, which, I
understand, is quite different from a random match probability. However, given
all the other evidence in this case, including the opinion of Mr. Mellis
that a person was sitting on this chair before it was overturned and was
bleeding into the cushion as he was sitting on it, and the evidence from the
autopsy that Mr. Rozen had stab wounds to his inner thighs near his groin
that correspond with these bloodstains, I am satisfied beyond a reasonable
doubt that Mr. Rozen sat in this chair and was bleeding from stab wounds
to his inner thighs onto the chair and its cushion as he sat there.

[
307
]

Third, Mr. Mellis testified that in his opinion the bloodstains
at location AA next to the front door were expirated blood, projected from the
nose or mouth, and that there were semi-circular stains above the deadbolt knob
on the front door, indicating a turning motion. Mr. Poon's evidence was
that the blood at AA was a single-source male profile that matches Mr. Rozen.
The blood on the doorknob and deadbolt knob were a mixed male profile with
components matching Marc Rozen and Mr. Newman. The evidence from the
autopsy indicates the gunshot wound that penetrated Mr. Rozen's sinus
cavity could cause bleeding into the nasal and oral cavity, and Dr. Lee
found aspirated blood in Mr. Rozen's trachea and lungs caused by breathing
in some blood. Taking all this evidence together, I find that Mr. Rozen
was at the front door trying to leave the apartment after he had been shot and
the bullet had lodged in his maxillary sinus below his left eye, and he was
prevented from leaving by Mr. Newman.

[
308
]

I next consider the evidence in relation to the guns. The forensic
evidence shows that two firearms were used in the assault on Marc Rozen. I am
satisfied that the Beretta (Exhibit 236) with the silencer (Exhibit 240) was
used to fire the bullets that were marked as Exhibits 72, 73, and 74, which I
shall henceforth simply refer to as bullet 72, bullet 73, and so on.

[
309
]

I am satisfied that bullet 72 was fired from a location outside the
purple room, into the purple room, ricocheting off the floor causing the divot
in the floor, and then striking Mr. Rozen in his left hand.

[
310
]

Bullet 73 was fired at a distance and is the bullet that was
recovered from the maxillary sinus below the left eye. It would have been fired
when Mr. Rozen was turned away from the shooter, as the trajectory was
from back to front. It was a serious wound that would cause blood loss and
death.

[
311
]

Bullet 74 was recovered from Mr. Rozen's shoulder, and fired
from a distance of more than two or three feet, and would not have caused
immediate death by itself.

[
312
]

Bullets 119 and 154 were found on the stove and in the closet wall. They
were both fired by the Beretta. The cartridge case found in the track of the
sliding doors off the dining room was also fired by the Beretta.

[
313
]

Bullet 62 was fired from a different gun. It was fired from the
Ruger.

The Shot from the Ruger

[
314
]

While I cannot say for certain who fired the shots from the Beretta,
I am satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Newman fired bullet 62
from the Ruger, and in doing so, he caused the death of Mr. Rozen. I base
this conclusion not on any single piece of evidence or any single
circumstantial inference. With respect to any single circumstance, taken in
isolation, one might find an innocent explanation is possible. But when all of
the evidence and all of the circumstances are considered together, I find that
the only reasonable conclusion is that Mr. Newman fired bullet 62 from the
Ruger into the back of Mr. Rozen's head. I am satisfied of this beyond a
reasonable doubt, based on the cumulative effect of all the evidence led by the
Crown and the defence.

[
315
]

While this conclusion is based on all the evidence, among the most
significant circumstances are the following.

[
316
]

The forensic evidence, which I accept, is that bullet 62 was fired
by the Ruger, Exhibit 238. The bullet was seized when it rolled off from Mr. Rozen's
left neck area as the coroner was putting his body into the body bag. The place
where the bullet was found is adjacent to the location that Dr. Lee said
was the exit wound of the gunshot to the back of Mr. Rozen's head. I
accept Dr. Lee's evidence that the shot causing this wound was fired at a
close range of one to two inches to the back of the head, but the gun was not
in contact with the skin. The trajectory was from back to front, from right to
left, and downward. I accept Dr. Lee's opinion that this gunshot
penetrated the brain stem, would have been almost immediately fatal, and that Mr. Rozen
would not have moved afterward.

[
317
]

I also accept Dr. Lee's evidence that the post-mortem lividity
established that Mr. Rozen died on his back at a time when he had very
little blood left in him, suggesting that Mr. Rozen had already lost
extensive amounts of blood from the knife wounds before he was shot in the back
of the head by the Ruger.

[
318
]

The photographs marked Exhibit 34 show the condition of the
apartment on January 6, 2004, when the police arrived. Photographs A21 and A23
show the position of Mr. Rozen's body before it was removed by the coroner.
Mr. Rozen was lying on his back on the living room rug. His head and left
arm were on top of the overturned plant, indicating that the plant must have
been overturned at some earlier point in the struggle. Mr. Rozen's body
was positioned diagonally on the rug, with his feet at or near the southeast
corner of that rug, and his head in the direction of the northwest corner.

[
319
]

This area is also shown in the photographs at pages 3 and 4 of
Exhibit 178. Mr. Mellis testified that bloodstain A is a heavy, congealed
soak stain on the living room rug caused by bleeding from Mr. Rozen. Bloodstain
B on the front of the living room sofa was a fabric wipe stain from bloody
clothing. Bloodstain D was congealed blood with multiple swipes from sliding a
bloody object, such as Mr. Rozen's feet. Mr. Mellis also found a
sockfoot impression not far from the southeast corner of the living room rug,
which he circled on the photographs at pages 3 and 4 of Exhibit 178.

[
320
]

Mr. Mellis testified that in his opinion, the bloodstains
marked A, B, and D were all created during the last movements and stationary
position of Marc Rozen when he died.

[
321
]

Since the gunshot wound from the bullet marked Exhibit 62 was almost
immediately fatal, and since Mr. Rozen would not have moved after
suffering that wound, we can infer that at the time that shot was fired, Mr. Rozen
must have been positioned at or near the southeast corner of the living room
rug, facing in a generally southward direction. Since the gunshot was fired at
the back of his head from a distance of two to three inches, his assailant must
have been standing on the living room rug immediately behind him, and close to
the bloodstain marked B on the sofa. This is within a few feet of the sockfoot
print on the hardwood floor that Mr. Mellis circled on the photographs at
pages 3 and 4 of Exhibit 178.

[
322
]

The DNA evidence indicates that the bloodstain marked B on the sofa
had a component that matched Mr. Newman. There was also a component that
matched Mr. Rozen.

[
323
]

The trajectory of the Ruger gunshot wound was from back to front,
from right to left, and downward. This would be consistent with someone
standing behind Mr. Rozen, holding the Ruger in his right hand, and firing
into the back of Mr. Rozen's head. Mr. Newman testified that he is
right-handed.

[
324
]

Mr. Newman's DNA was found not only on one, but rather on two
different places on the Ruger. The forensic evidence is that a single source
male DNA profile was located on the safety and end of the slide of the Ruger,
and the same male profile was found on the end and inside of the Ruger's barrel.
Hiron Poon testified that it matched Mr. Newman's DNA profile.

[
325
]

The Ruger and the Beretta were found in Mr. Newman's residence
in Ontario in 2007. Mr. Newman admitted to the police in Ontario that the
guns in his residence were his and no one else's. We know from Mr. Newman's
testimony that he is the one who took the guns from Mr. Rozen's apartment
after the killing, and that he kept them until they were found in his residence
by the York Regional Police.

[
326
]

Finally, a piece of chewing gum was found on the top side of the
shirt Mr. Rozen was wearing when the police found him lying on his back in
the living room. The DNA on that chewing gum matched Mr. Newman.

[
327
]

From these circumstances, and from a consideration of all the
evidence, I find beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Newman fired the Ruger
at close range to the back of Mr. Rozen's head and thereby caused his
death. I find that this conclusion is consistent with the totality of the
evidence, and that it is the only reasonable conclusion to be drawn from the
whole of the evidence.

Homicide and Murder

[
328
]

Subject to the defence of self-defence, which I shall discuss in a
moment, firing the Ruger at Mr. Rozen was an unlawful act which caused Mr. Rozen's
death. It is therefore culpable homicide as defined by
s. 222
of the
Criminal
Code
.

[
329
]

Section 229
(a) of the
Criminal Code

defines murder. It provides:

229. Culpable homicide is murder

(a) where the person who causes the death of
a human being

(i) means to cause
his death, or

(ii) means to cause him bodily harm that he
knows is likely to cause his death, and is reckless whether death ensues or
not;

[
330
]

There is no suggestion in the evidence that intoxication by alcohol
or drugs played any role in this killing, and there is no evidence of any other
circumstance that would detract from the common-sense inference that a sane and
sober person normally intends the reasonable and probable consequences of his
acts. The reasonable and probable consequence of firing the Ruger at close
range to Mr. Rozen's head is that it would cause death, and I find that
the Crown has proven beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Newman had that
intention and that he committed the murder of Mr. Rozen under
s. 229
(a)(i).
In addition, there can be no doubt that in firing the Ruger as he did, Mr. Newman
meant to cause Mr. Rozen bodily harm that he knew was likely to cause
death and was reckless whether death ensued or not, and his culpability for
murder is established under
s. 229
(a)(ii) as well.

The Knife Wounds

[
331
]

In addition, I find beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Newman
also caused most, if not all, of the 62 to 63 cuts and stab wounds to Mr. Rozen.
This is clear from the forensic evidence of Mr. Rozen's blood and DNA
found on Mr. Newman's clothing, and the blood and DNA of Mr. Newman
that was found on Mr. Rozen and his clothing. There is no evidence of any
blood on the unknown woman or on the unknown male, if indeed there was such a
male in the apartment. The hypothesis that there was an unknown male in the
apartment is based largely on the evidence of Mr. Cosovic that some time
after January 6, 2004, he recalled having seen a man and a woman leave the
building who were not tenants. Yet on his testimony, there is no evidence that
they had any blood on them or on their clothing and there is no indication that
they were injured in any way. The evidence satisfies me beyond a reasonable
doubt that the struggle involving a knife or knives was a struggle between Mr. Rozen
and Mr. Newman, and not others.

[
332
]

The evidence of Dr. Lee was that the cause of death included
the knife wounds as well as the gunshot wounds. I find that the knife wounds
inflicted by Mr. Newman were an unlawful act and a substantial
contributing cause of death beyond the
de minimus
range. I am satisfied
from the number, location, and severity of those knife wounds that Mr. Newman
inflicted them with the intention of causing Mr. Rozen bodily harm that he
knew was likely to cause death and was reckless whether death ensued or not.
Mr. Newman's culpability for murder is therefore established under

s. 229
(a)(ii) based on the knife wounds, even apart from the gunshot
wounds.

Self-Defence

[
333
]

I have not yet discussed self-defence. On Mr. Newman's
account of the case, the defence of self-defence would not arise, because he
testified that Mr. Rozen did not assault him. Nevertheless, his counsel
submits that self-defence must be considered in the alternative. He submits
that the two sections of the
Criminal Code
that need to be considered
are
ss. 34(1)
and
34(2)
. Those sections provide:

34. (1) Everyone who is unlawfully assaulted
without having provoked the assault is justified in repelling force by force if
the force he uses is not intended to cause death or grievous bodily harm and is
no more than is necessary to enable him to defend himself.

(2) Everyone who is unlawfully assaulted and
who causes death or grievous bodily harm in repelling the assault is justified
if

(a) he causes it
under reasonable apprehension of death or grievous bodily harm from the
violence with which the assault was originally made or with which the assailant
pursues his purposes; and

(b) he believes, on reasonable grounds,
that he cannot otherwise preserve himself from death or grievous bodily harm.

[
334
]

I find it difficult to see how there can be an air of reality to the
defence of self-defence in this case, in light of the fact that Mr. Newman
testified that he was never unlawfully assaulted by Mr. Rozen, a
proposition that I accept as true. Nevertheless, Crown counsel agrees with the
defence that I must consider self-defence in light of the decision of our Court
of Appeal in
R. v. Brar
,
2009 BCCA 585
, 250 C.C.C. (3d) 198.

[
335
]

In support of the self-defence submission, defence counsel points to
Mr. Newman's injuries. Mr. Newman testified that he received injuries
to his head, his hands, and his neck. He claims that the injuries to his neck
included a gunshot wound.

[
336
]

I am skeptical that Mr. Newman in fact received a gunshot wound.
Dr. Gentis testified that he did not believe the wound to the neck was
from a gunshot. If he had thought it was from a gunshot, he would have called
the police. The defence attempts to explain this away by the evidence of Mr. Krezanski
that a friend, Mr. Chan, extracted the bullet from Mr. Newman's neck
with tweezers before going to see Dr. Gentis. Yet Mr. Krezanski said
he was five feet away and never actually saw the bullet in Mr. Newman's
neck. He said he only saw a bullet after Mr. Chan had extracted it.
Mr. Chan was not called as a witness because he has since died. The bullet
was never produced, because Mr. Newman said he left it in Mexico.

[
337
]

I agree with the submission of the Crown that if Mr. Newman had
been shot from the same gun that shot Mr. Rozen, it is very unlikely that
it would have been possible for a layperson like Mr. Chan to extract the
bullet from his neck simply by using tweezers. In my view, it is much more
likely that all of Mr. Newman's injuries were knife wounds.

[
338
]

Nevertheless, I cannot rule out the possibility of a gunshot wound
to Mr. Newman beyond a reasonable doubt. If it was a gunshot wound, then I
find that it must have been an accident, caused by careless use of one of Mr. Newman's
own firearms, either by himself or by one of his companions who were joining
him in the assault on Mr. Rozen. We already have evidence of the Beretta
being carelessly fired in the apartment, namely, the bullet that was fired into
the wall of the closet, and the bullet that ricocheted off the floor at the
entrance to the purple room causing the divot.

[
339
]

As to Mr. Newman's other injuries, I find that they were not as
serious as Mr. Newman claimed during his testimony. The fact that Mr. Newman
currently has scars on his hands and head does not demonstrate that these are a
result of the injuries he suffered on January 6, 2004. Constable Kelly saw Mr. Newman
in St. Paul's Hospital one year later on January 27, 2005, where he was
being treated for a hand injury. Sergeant Chan testified that he saw Mr. Newman
on March 17, 2005, and he had a fresh injury to his left hand. As well, Mr. Finewax
testified that Mr. Newman told him that his scars were from a knife wound
when he was a kid. Finally, Dr. Gentis testified that when he treated Mr. Newman,
the only significant injury was to his neck. He said all the other injuries
were superficial. He said the injuries to the hands would not impair their
function.

[
340
]

I find that the Crown has proven beyond a reasonable doubt that no
defence of self-defence arises under s. 34(1), because the evidence
establishes that Mr. Newman was not unlawfully assaulted by Mr. Rozen
without having provoked the assault. Mr. Rozen was in his own home. He had
no reason to launch an unprovoked attack against the strangers to whom he was
trying to sell the ring. While it is unclear exactly how the struggle began, it
is simply preposterous to propose that Mr. Rozen assaulted Mr. Newman
without provocation. The evidence, including Mr. Newman's own testimony,
is entirely to the contrary. I find that whatever injuries Mr. Newman may
have suffered at the hands of Mr. Rozen were the result of Mr. Rozen
trying to defend himself from the attack upon himself, and not the other way
around.

[
341
]

As well, the evidence is clear that more force was used than was
necessary to enable Mr. Newman to defend himself. The gunshot wounds and
the 62 to 63 stab wounds were clearly excessive, even taking into account the
dictum that a man under assault cannot be expected to weigh to a nicety the
required degree of responsive force.

[
342
]

As to s. 34(2), the defence must fail because there is no
evidence that Mr. Newman was under an apprehension of death or grievous
bodily harm from Mr. Rozen's original violence, or that any such
apprehension was reasonable. There is no evidence that Mr. Newman believed
that he could not otherwise preserve himself than by killing Mr. Rozen. The
evidence is all to the contrary. Mr. Newman testified that he believed Mr. Rozen
was trying to save his, that is Mr. Newman's, life. As well, the evidence
establishes that Mr. Newman did not have reasonable grounds for believing
that he could not otherwise preserve himself. He could have simply left the
apartment. On his own testimony, there were clear opportunities for him to
leave.

[
343
]

Finally, it is significant that the evidence of the neighbours
supports the view that it was Mr. Rozen who was being unlawfully assaulted
in his apartment rather than the other way around. Barbara Darovski said she
heard the word "Help" only once, and she was almost sure it was Marc
Rozen's voice. Mr. Prodanuk recognized Marc Rozen's voice saying,
"Why are you doing this to me?" This confirms that it was Mr. Rozen
who was unlawfully assaulted by the others in his apartment, and the only
injuries he caused were when he was trying to defend himself from them.

[
344
]

Accordingly, I find that the Crown has proven against Mr. Newman
all the essential elements of murder and has disproved any defence beyond a
reasonable doubt. I therefore find Mr. Newman guilty of murder.

First or Second Degree

[
345
]

I must now go on to consider whether the Crown
has proven that the murder is first degree. The Crown relies on
s. 231(5)

of the
Criminal Code
, which provides:

231 (5) Irrespective of whether a murder is
planned and deliberate on the part of any person, murder is first degree murder
in respect of a person when the death is caused by that person while committing
or attempting to commit an offence under one of the following sections:

. . .

(e) section 279
(kidnapping and forcible confinement);

[
346
]

The offence of forcible confinement under s. 279 requires proof
that the accused intentionally and without lawful authority deprived another
person without his consent of his liberty to move from one place to another:
R.
v. Luxton
,
1990 CanLII 83 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 711. This does not require proof of total
physical restraint:
R. v. Gratton

(1985), 18 C.C.C, (3d) 462 (Ont.
C.A.)
.

[
347
]

In this case, I am satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Rozen
was forcibly confined by his attackers, and particularly by Mr. Newman. This
occurred at least three times during the altercation. One time relates to the
events at the front door. I have already referred to the evidence that Mr. Rozen
was at the front door expirating blood on the wall next to the door after he
had been shot. The bloodstains around the deadbolt satisfy me beyond a
reasonable doubt that he was trying to leave the apartment, but was prevented
from doing so by Mr. Newman.

[
348
]

I am also satisfied that Mr. Rozen was forcibly confined as he
sat in the chair that was found overturned in the living room/dining room. The
blood-soaked cushion and bloodstain on the front of that chair, coupled with
the evidence of Mr. Mellis and the autopsy evidence, satisfy me beyond a
reasonable doubt that Mr. Rozen was forced to sit in this chair and was
bleeding from stab wounds to his inner thighs onto the chair and its cushion as
he sat there. I find this was a confinement, because a person being attacked as
Mr. Rozen was being attacked would not willingly assume the submissive and
defenceless position of sitting in a chair while the assault was ongoing. This
is reinforced by the stab wounds to his inner thighs, which are in a location
that an attacker would not have access to unless the victim were first rendered
defenceless.

[
349
]

Finally, I find that Mr. Rozen was unlawfully confined when he
was shot from a distance of one or two inches in the back of the head. The
trajectory was downward and from back to front, meaning that the shooter was
above and behind Mr. Rozen when shooting him at very close range in the
back of the head. The downward direction of the shot indicates that Mr. Rozen
was in a submissive and helpless position. Dr. Lee testified that this
shot would have been almost instantly fatal. It is the type of shot that brings
to mind an execution. It is difficult to imagine a more dramatic example of one
person exercising total domination over another. I find that Mr. Rozen was
being unlawfully confined when that shot was fired.

[
350
]

I find that the acts causing Mr. Rozen's death and the acts
constituting the offence of unlawful confinement all form part of a continuous
sequence of events making up a single transaction, and the murder was therefore
committed while committing or attempting to commit the offence of unlawful
confinement:
R. v. Paré
,
1987 CanLII 1 (SCC)
, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 618. The acts of confinement
go beyond those acts that are simply inherent in the killing itself:
R. v.
Kimberley
(2001),
2001 CanLII 24120 (ON CA)
, 157 C.C.C. (3d) 129 (Ont. C.A.). Both by his firing of
the Ruger and by his infliction of knife injuries, Mr. Newman's actions
formed an "essential, substantial and integral part of the killing"
of Mr. Rozen within the meaning of that phrase in
R. v. Harbottle
,

1993 CanLII 71 (SCC)
, [1993] 3 S.C.R. 306. His acts are of such a nature that they must be regarded
as a substantial and integral cause of the death.

[
351
]

In short, I find that Mr. Newman caused the death of Mr. Rozen
while committing or attempting to commit the offence of forcible confinement,
and that the Crown has proven beyond a reasonable doubt all the elements of
first degree murder. I find that the Crown has proven beyond a reasonable doubt
that the defence of self-defence cannot succeed. The evidence adduced by the
defence does not raise any reasonable doubt in my mind of Mr. Newman's
guilt.

[
352
]

Mr. Newman, would you please stand.

[
353
]

I find you, Michael Bruce Newman, guilty as charged of the first
degree murder of Marc Rozen.
